title: Skyroot's Vikram-1 Makes History as India's First Private Orbital Rocket
excerpt: Hyderabad-based Skyroot Aerospace completed Mission Aagaman on Saturday, launching a four-stage, carbon-composite rocket into a 450 km orbit from Sriharikota — the first time a privately built Indian vehicle has reached space.
body:
• Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 successfully completed its maiden orbital flight from Sriharikota on July 18, making it the first privately built Indian rocket to reach orbit.
  • Mission Aagaman deployed payloads from domestic and international customers into a 450 km Low Earth Orbit after completing all four stages in under 10 minutes.
  • Founded by former ISRO scientists, the Hyderabad-based startup has reached a $1.1 billion valuation and plans up to two more Vikram-1 launches this year.
  • The milestone follows India's 2023 space policy reforms that opened orbital launch activities to private companies under IN-SPACe oversight.

Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 rocket lifted off from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota on Saturday, completing India's first privately developed orbital mission and marking a turning point for the country's commercial space industry.

The seven-storey-tall launch vehicle, designated Mission Aagaman — meaning "arrival" — launched at 12:05 PM IST after a 35-minute hold caused by weather conditions and last-minute technical checks, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. All four stages completed in under 10 minutes, successfully injecting multiple payloads into a 450 km Low Earth Orbit.

A Rocket Built From Scratch

Vikram-1 is engineered with an all-carbon-composite airframe and 3D-printed engines — firsts for an Indian launch vehicle. The four-stage design combines three solid-propellant stages with a liquid-propellant orbital adjustment module, capable of carrying up to 480 kg to LEO and 290 kg to Sun Synchronous Orbit, according to Inc42.

The maiden flight validated propulsion, avionics, telemetry, guidance, navigation, and stage separation systems under actual flight conditions. It carried technology demonstration payloads from Grahaa Space, Cosmoserve, DCubed, and Skyroot's own SCOPE experiment, alongside commercial cargo including a lab-grown diamond artwork called "Diamond Lotus" from Bengaluru-based Cosmos Diamonds.

"The first-ever Indian private sector launch has been successfully completed. Not only did it meet the mission objectives, and deployed all the payloads as intended."

— Chairperson, IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre)

From ISRO Labs to Unicorn Status

Skyroot was founded in 2018 by Pawan Kumar Chandana and Naga Bharath Daka, both former ISRO scientists who bet that India's space sector needed private launch capability alongside the government's established programme. Their first milestone came in November 2022 with Vikram-S, a suborbital technology demonstrator that made Skyroot the first Indian private company to launch a rocket of any kind.

The company raised $60 million two months before the launch in a round co-led by Sherpalo Ventures and GIC at a pre-money valuation of $1.1 billion, making it India's first spacetech unicorn. Its 2 lakh sq ft Infinity Campus in Hyderabad now has the manufacturing capacity to produce one orbital rocket per month.

Policy Reforms Pay Off

Saturday's launch is arguably the most visible outcome of India's 2023 space policy reforms, which opened launch activities to private companies under the supervision of IN-SPACe. Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who sent a handwritten postcard reading "Vande Mataram" as one of the mission's symbolic payloads, called Vikram-1's flight a "historic new frontier" for India's space journey and spoke with the Skyroot team by phone after the successful mission.

"A historic new frontier for India's space journey! This mission highlights the talent, determination and entrepreneurial spirit of our youth."

— Prime Minister Narendra Modi, via post on X

With India's spacetech sector projected to reach $77 billion by 2030, the successful mission positions Skyroot as a credible commercial launch provider in the fast-growing global small satellite market — a segment long dominated by SpaceX's rideshare programme and Rocket Lab in the West.

What Comes Next

Skyroot plans up to two more Vikram-1 flights before the end of 2026, transitioning from test flights to commercial satellite deployments. The company is also developing Vikram-1U, an upgraded variant with strap-on boosters expected in Q1 2027, and Vikram-2, a one-tonne-class vehicle with a cryogenic upper stage for heavier payloads.

For the Indian diaspora watching from abroad, Saturday's launch carries a familiar echo: a generation of engineers and entrepreneurs, many of whom trained at ISRO or IITs before building careers overseas, now seeing India's private sector match capabilities that were once the exclusive domain of state agencies — and doing so with technology that stands up to global competition.
